title: How do you read a chart in a case interview and find the insight?
description: Exhibits are where cases are won or lost. A five-step routine for turning any chart into an insight.
hook: You read a case chart by checking its frame first (title, axes and units, legend, footnote), then finding the one thing that stands out, putting a number on it, linking it to the client's goal and proposing a next step. Interviewers do not want a description of everything on the page. They want the single insight that matters for the decision, and this five-step routine gets you there in under a minute.
body:
In this guide

  • What the interviewer is testing
  • Step 1: ask for a moment and read the frame
  • Step 2: find what stands out
  • Step 3: quantify it
  • Step 4: link it to the goal
  • Step 5: say the next step
  • The routine in one answer
  • What to look for in each chart type
  • Common mistakes
  • Check yourself
  • Where to practise next

What the interviewer is testing

An exhibit in a case is a small test of the job itself. Consultants spend much of their time turning data into a sentence a client can act on. When the interviewer hands you a chart, they are checking whether you read it accurately, whether you can separate the signal from the noise, and whether you connect it back to the problem without being prompted.

The most common failure is description: reading out what the chart shows, line by line, and stopping there. Everything below is designed to move you from description to insight.

Step 1: ask for a moment and read the frame

Say "May I take a moment to look at this?" It is a normal request, and a short, purposeful silence while you read is better than talking before you understand the chart. Then read the frame in this order:

  • Title: what the chart claims to show, and for which period.
  • Axes and units: dollars or units, thousands or millions, absolute values or percentages, nominal or real.
  • Legend: which colour or line is which, and whether any series is the client.
  • Footnote: exclusions and definitions. Notes such as "excludes stores opened this year" or "values in real terms" can change the whole story.

Checking units and footnotes first is what stops you making a confident claim that is off by a factor of 1,000 or built on the wrong definition.

Step 2: find what stands out

Most charts in cases are built around one or two insights. Look for four things:

  • The biggest number: the largest segment, cost or region.
  • The biggest change: the steepest rise or fall.
  • A crossing point: where demand overtakes supply, or a competitor overtakes the client.
  • An outlier: the one store, product or year that does not fit the pattern.

The difference between description and insight is easy to hear:

Weak: "This shows supply and demand from 2026 to 2030."
Strong: "Demand overtakes supply from 2028, and by 2030 there's a 20% shortfall."

Step 3: quantify it

If a number on the chart can be turned into something more useful, such as a percentage, a gap, a share or a growth rate, do it without being asked. "Sales in the North fell" is an observation. "The North fell by $12M, more than the whole company's decline" is an insight.

Always check percentages against their bases. Suppose a chart shows sales up 20% in the North and 5% in the South. Before calling the North the growth engine, look at size. If North revenue was $1M, its increase is $200k. If South revenue was $20M, its 5% increase is $1M. The smaller percentage created five times more growth in dollars.

For help with the arithmetic itself, the case maths cheat sheet has the shortcuts on one page.

Step 4: link it to the goal

Connect the number to the question at the top of your page: "...which matters because the client has committed to supplying 120,000 tonnes by 2030." If you cannot say why the insight matters for the client's decision, you have not finished reading the chart.

Step 5: say the next step

End by proposing where to go next. This is how you drive the case rather than waiting to be led: "I'd like to understand why the North fell. Do we have data on store count or competitor openings there?"

Also ask what the chart cannot tell you. Is the growth profitable? Is the market growing just as fast? Is it repeatable or a one-off? Raising one of these shows judgement, not just reading ability.

The routine in one answer

Here is a chart of bed occupancy across a client's 12 hospitals, read using all five steps (the numbers are illustrative):

"This shows bed occupancy for each of the client's 12 hospitals last year (read). Most sit between 60% and 78%, but three newer hospitals are around 40% (find). Those three pull the simple average down to 62%, against a 75% benchmark (quantify). That matters because filling empty beds is the cheapest way for the client to grow (link). I'd like to understand why those three are empty: is it a shortage of doctors, or weak referrals from local GPs? (next step)"

It takes about 30 seconds to say, and every sentence earns its place. A weak version of the same answer would list several hospitals' occupancy figures and stop.

What to look for in each chart type

ChartLook forRead more
WaterfallThe one or two bars that explain most of the changeWaterfall charts
LineTurning points, gaps between lines, growth ratesLine charts
Stacked barWhich segment is changing the mixStacked bars
ScatterThe trend and the points far from itScatter plots
TableThe row or column that breaks the patternTables of numbers

Common mistakes

  • Describing instead of concluding. Fix: lead with the insight sentence, then support it with numbers.
  • Skipping the units or footnote. Fix: read the frame first, every time, even when you are in a hurry.
  • Comparing percentages without bases. Fix: convert to dollars or units before saying which segment matters most.
  • Calculating everything. Fix: quantify the one or two numbers that support your insight, not every bar.
  • Stopping at the insight. Fix: always finish with the link to the goal and a next step.

Check yourself

Have a go at each one before you open the answer.

1. What should you read before drawing any conclusion from a chart?

  • Only the biggest bar
  • Title, axes, units, legend and footnote
  • Nothing: speed matters most
Show the answer

Title, axes, units, legend and footnote. Units and footnotes change the meaning of a chart more often than you would think.

2. Which is an insight rather than a description?

  • "The chart shows sales by region."
  • "Sales fell in every region."
  • "Two-thirds of the drop comes from one region, the North."
Show the answer

"Two-thirds of the drop comes from one region, the North." It locates the problem, quantifies it and tells you where to dig next.

3. Try it out loud: sales by region, year 1 to year 2 ($M): North 40 to 28, South 35 to 36, West 25 to 26. Give one insight with a number, and say where you would look next.

Give yourself 60 seconds.

Show a strong answer

"Total sales fell from $100M to $90M, a 10% drop. But the North alone fell by $12M, a 30% fall and more than the entire decline, while the South and West each grew by $1M. So this is a North problem, not a company-wide one. Next I'd look at what changed in the North: a new competitor, store closures or the loss of a key customer."
